name: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis
aliases: Langerhans cell granulomatosis of the lung

reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine / European Respiratory Monograph on rare lung disease
clinicalPearls: Almost exclusively a disease of young to middle-aged current smokers, with a strong causal link to cigarette smoke
Presents with dry cough and breathlessness, and spontaneous pneumothorax is a common and sometimes recurrent presenting event
High-resolution CT shows a combination of nodules and bizarre, thick-walled and later thin-walled cysts, with striking upper- and mid-zone predominance and relative sparing of the costophrenic angles
Disease evolves over time from cellular nodules through cavitating nodules to cysts, reflecting bronchiolocentric Langerhans cell infiltration and destruction
Many cases carry activating BRAF V600E or other MAP-kinase pathway mutations, placing PLCH within the spectrum of clonal histiocytic neoplasms
Smoking cessation is the single most important intervention and can lead to stabilisation or regression
Extrapulmonary involvement such as diabetes insipidus, bone lesions, or skin disease should be sought as it changes management
Progressive disease may be treated with systemic therapy, and targeted therapy is considered when a driver mutation is present
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis is driven by the accumulation of clonal, activated Langerhans-type dendritic cells around the small airways, almost always in response to cigarette smoke. These CD1a-positive, Langerin-positive cells, frequently harbouring activating mutations of the MAP-kinase pathway such as BRAF V600E, recruit eosinophils and other inflammatory cells to form bronchiolocentric nodules. Progressive inflammation destroys the distal bronchioles and adjacent alveoli, so the nodules cavitate and coalesce into cysts, producing the characteristic upper-zone cystic-nodular architecture and, over time, airflow obstruction and pulmonary hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic cystic disease or other diffuse cystic lung disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT to identify the upper-zone nodular and cystic pattern with basal sparing
Careful smoking history and counselling as both diagnostic clue and therapeutic lever
Pulmonary function tests, often showing reduced diffusing capacity with obstructive or mixed defects
Bronchoalveolar lavage or lung biopsy demonstrating CD1a/Langerin-positive Langerhans cells when confirmation is needed
BRAF V600E and other MAP-kinase mutation testing on biopsy material
Assessment for extrapulmonary disease including pituitary imaging, skeletal survey, and skin examination
redFlags: Features of pulmonary hypertension complicating advanced cystic disease
New polyuria/polydipsia suggesting pituitary involvement with diabetes insipidus
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable; many patients stabilise or improve after stopping smoking, but some progress to extensive cystic destruction, respiratory failure, and pulmonary hypertension, and continued smoking is associated with worse outcomes.
pitfalls: Failing to take a detailed smoking history and to make cessation the cornerstone of management
Misreading the cystic pattern as emphysema or lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Overlooking extrapulmonary manifestations such as diabetes insipidus or bone lesions
Not testing for a targetable driver mutation in progressive disease
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
European Respiratory Society statement on pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis
management: Prioritise complete and sustained smoking cessation, which can lead to stabilisation or regression and is the cornerstone of care
Use corticosteroids for progressive or symptomatic nodular disease
Offer cladribine or other chemotherapy, and BRAF or MEK inhibitors where an activating MAP-kinase mutation is present, for progressive or multisystem disease
Treat recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax with drainage and pleurodesis
Provide supportive oxygen for hypoxaemia and pulmonary rehabilitation, and manage secondary pulmonary hypertension
Screen for extrapulmonary involvement and monitor with serial lung function and high-resolution CT
Refer end-stage disease with respiratory failure for lung transplantation
